episode_thesis: Trend following lost money in 2025 because the uncertainty was man-made (tariffs, policy), was switched on and off quickly by policy, and was resolved positively, so sell-offs reversed without the slow behavioural follow-through that trend needs. Rzepczynski's lesson is that crisis alpha depends on the type of crisis, that trend is long long-term volatility but short short-term volatility (stops), and that Treasuries proved a fickle safe asset, so a dynamic long/short strategy such as trend can serve as a substitute safe asset over long horizons.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: The ChatGPT answer that trend does better in high-vol periods rests on a listener's shortcut with no stress test; Mark replies that the answer is more nuanced and depends on model type.
Mark cites a recent paper on gold across crisis types, a paper on riding bubbles and ML currency work without naming them; the claims cannot be checked from the transcript.
The knock-out option description of trend (long long-term vol, short short-term vol) is an analogy; no test or statistics are offered.
The link between higher US policy uncertainty and capital flowing to Europe is asserted as an explanation without flow data.
Mark said uncertainty was positively resolved but also says it is still elevated and only partially resolved; the point at which the reversal ends is unclear.

Niels cites the 9.5% one-day rise on a presidential call to buy as contradicting the 'nothing good happens below the 200-day average' maxim, while Mark attributes trend losses to reversals and intraday stop-outs; the relative weight of each is not quantified.
UK 1925 to 1975 analogy for the US dollar is illustrative only; the timing and trigger of any US bailout are not supported.
Berkshire drawdowns and the claim that deep drawdowns do not matter are used as encouragement rather than evidence for trend.
Leverage-based Bitcoin lending critique rests on one executive's comments; the point about system fragility is general.
Dispersion is described as up in 2025 but also as low because of a single driver; the two statements are about different periods (April vs the year).
Financial stress readings (ECB, banks, St. Louis Fed) are described qualitatively only.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Inputs the speakers treat as leading for trend returns: whether uncertainty resolves negatively (follow-through) or positively (reversal); the pace of policy reversals; VIX level versus its moving average; dispersion and correlation-network tightness; newspaper uncertainty indices (trade, policy); financial stress indices; stock-bond correlation and long yields (30y above 5%, 10y above 4.5%); US deficits. Horizon is weeks to months for trend losses, and decades for evaluating trend as a safe asset.
reader_inferences: (reader) Mark's framework implies trend does best when uncertainty resolves negatively and slowly, and worst for fast-reversing man-made shocks; this is a testable regime hypothesis that no one tests on air.
(reader) The 'safe asset' definition (low or negative correlation when markets fall) is operational and could be tested for trend, Treasuries and gold across crisis types.
(reader) The long convexity advice conflicts with the claim that trend is short short-term vol; the way out is that dedicated options differ from trend with stops.
(reader) The leverage warning is about vol targeting without floors; the host's vol floor is the practical fix.
